lessons.t: Build for the model six months out
lessons.html:
A feature you start today ships in a quarter and lives for years. The model it runs on will be replaced several times in that period. So the planning question is what the product should look like when the model is much better and cheaper than the one you are testing with.

The trend lines

Two measurements are worth knowing, with their caveats. METR measured the length of software tasks, by how long a skilled human takes, that models complete with 50% success. Over roughly six years to early 2025 that horizon doubled about every seven months, and faster in the most recent data. METR is clear that the exact numbers depend on its task suite. Epoch AI found in March 2025 that the price of reaching a fixed level of performance fell between 9× and 900× per year depending on the benchmark. Neither trend is guaranteed to continue. Both say that planning against today’s model is planning against the floor.

The Bitter Lesson, applied to products

Rich Sutton’s 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson argues that, across 70 years of AI research, general methods that scale with computation have beaten methods built on hand-coded human knowledge, and by a large margin. Researchers kept building clever domain-specific structure that helped in the short term and was then overtaken by brute scale.

Product teams repeat the pattern. They build elaborate prompt chains to decompose reasoning the model can’t yet do in one pass, regex post-processors to fix formatting, hand-written routing trees and retrieval tricks for short context windows. Each works. Each is overtaken by the next model, and then becomes a constraint that makes the product worse than a plain call to the new model.

ScaffoldingTypeWhat happens when the model improves
Multi-step chains that break reasoning into small promptsCompensatingOften slower and worse than one call to a stronger model
Heavy few-shot examples and output repair to fix formatCompensatingStructured outputs and better instruction following make it redundant
Hand-built intent classifiers and routing treesCompensatingThe model routes itself, with more coverage
Integration with systems of record, permissions, auditDurableMore valuable, because a stronger model can do more with it
Evals and golden setsDurableThey tell you within days whether the new model is better
Review and approval UXDurableStill needed as the agent takes bigger actions
Proprietary context and feedback dataDurableThe model’s quality ceiling depends on it

Compensating scaffolding is often necessary to ship today. The rule is to build it thin, isolate it behind a clear interface, and record the eval case that justifies it, so you can delete it the week a model makes it unnecessary.

Rule of thumb

If a feature works 60–70% of the time on today’s best model and the failures are capability failures (reasoning, long context, tool use), design and instrument it now. Keep it behind a flag with its eval running against each new model. If the failures come from missing data or missing integration, a better model won’t fix them.

Some things don’t improve with the model. Prompt injection is structural (Chapter 12). Latency has floors from network and tool calls. Access to your customer’s data depends on contracts and integrations. Don’t bank on scale to solve those.

What changes for you

  • Label every piece of scaffolding in your design docs as compensating or durable, with the eval case that justifies each compensating piece.
  • Keep a capability watch list: features that fail today with a saved eval, rerun on every new model.
  • Price features against the cost curve you expect next year, but approve them only on today’s margin (Chapter 11).

lessons.t: Where moats actually come from: workflow, distribution, data, evals
lessons.html:
Every competitor can call the same models you can, usually within days of release. A product whose advantage is the model has no advantage. The question for any AI strategy is what a well-funded competitor would still lack if they had your model tomorrow.

SourceWhy it lastsHow it erodesTest question
WorkflowThe product sits where work happens: the system of record, approvals, permissions, integrations. Switching means retraining people and rewiring processes.A platform the customer already uses adds the same workflowIf we vanished, how many systems and habits would the customer have to change?
DistributionExisting users, seats, procurement relationships and bundles. An incumbent with good-enough AI often beats a startup with better AI.A lab or platform ships to more users than youHow do we reach the next 10,000 users, and what does it cost us versus a rival?
Proprietary dataOutcome data generated inside the workflow: which drafts were accepted, what was edited, what resolved the ticket.Public data and better base models close the gap on generic knowledgeDoes this data measurably improve our evals, and could a rival buy or scrape it?
EvalsA golden set that encodes domain judgement lets you adopt each new model within days, safely.Weak if nobody maintains it or it doesn’t match real usageHow long would it take us to switch models with confidence? How long for a rival?
Trust and complianceCertifications, audit trails, residency, and a record of safe operation (Chapter 12). Matters most in regulated buyers.Becomes table stakes as vendors catch upWhich deals do we win because of it?

Be precise about data

“Our data is our moat” is the most common and least examined claim in AI strategy. Volume of generic data rarely helps, because base models have read more than you have. Data matters when it is specific to your users’ decisions, generated by your product, and connected to outcomes. The data flywheel (Chapter 7) only exists if you can show that more usage produced a measurable eval improvement. If you can’t draw that line, call it an asset with option value and leave it out of the moat column.

Evals as speed

When a new model arrives, a team with a strong eval suite knows within a day or two whether it is better on their tasks, ships the switch, and captures the quality and cost gain. A team without one argues from demos for a month. Across many model releases, that difference in adoption speed compounds into a product gap. It is also invisible to competitors, which makes it one of the more defensible advantages a product team can build directly.

The test

Write down your moats, then imagine a competitor with the same model, twice your engineering team and none of your customers. List what they would still need a year to build. That list is your strategy. Anything not on it is an execution lead, and execution leads shrink with every model release.

What changes for you

  • Replace “AI-powered” in positioning docs with the specific workflow, distribution or data advantage, and the test question that proves it.
  • Ask for evidence when someone claims a data moat: which eval improved, by how much, from which data.
  • Fund eval maintenance as strategic work, with an owner and a refresh cadence.

lessons.t: Build, buy or wrap: platform risk and model dependence
lessons.html:
Every AI feature sits somewhere between buying a finished capability and building the whole stack. “Wrapper” gets used as an insult, but every product built on a model API wraps something. The real decisions are how thick the layer is where it matters, and how exposed you are to the companies underneath.

OptionWhat you ownGood fit whenMain risk
BuyConfiguration and rolloutThe capability is generic (meeting notes, translation, code completion) and not where you competeVendor roadmap and pricing; data leaves your control
WrapPrompts, context, UX, a thin harness over a model APISpeed matters and the value is in the experience and workflow fitThe model provider or a platform ships the same experience
Build the systemHarness, tools, retrieval, evals, routing across modelsThe task is core, multi-step, and needs your data and integrationsCost of ownership; compensating scaffolding that ages badly
Own the modelFine-tuned or self-hosted open-weight models, sometimes alongside APIsHigh volume, narrow task, strict residency or cost needsTrailing the frontier; retraining with each base model (Chapter 7)

Kinds of platform risk

  • The provider competes with you. Labs ship first-party apps and agents in coding, research, browsing and office work. If your product is the most obvious thing to build on their model, assume they will build it.
  • Terms move. Pricing, rate limits, data terms and usage policies change on the provider’s schedule.
  • Models retire. Pinned versions are deprecated on published timelines. A model you tuned your prompts around has a shelf life, and its replacement behaves differently (Chapter 10).
  • Distribution platforms gate you. Marketplaces, app stores and assistant integrations can change ranking, fees or access.

Mitigations that pay for themselves

  • A portable eval suite. The cheapest hedge. If you can score any model on your tasks in a day, switching is an engineering task instead of a crisis.
  • A thin model interface. Route calls through one layer so a second provider is a configuration change. Accept that full abstraction pushes you to the lowest common denominator. Use provider-specific features where the eval shows they pay, and record that dependency.
  • Run a second model in shadow on a sample of traffic so you always know your fallback’s quality and cost.
  • Own the workflow and the data path. The parts you own should be the parts a provider can’t easily ship: integrations, permissions, customer-specific context.

Decision rule

Buy what is generic. Wrap to learn fast. Build where the task is core and your data and integrations decide quality. Own a model only when volume, residency or cost makes the numbers work after counting the retraining you’ll do every time the frontier moves.

What changes for you

  • For each AI feature, write a platform-risk line: which provider dependencies exist, what happens if each changes, and the fallback.
  • Require that any new provider-specific feature comes with an eval showing its gain and a note on the exit cost.
  • Track deprecation dates for every pinned model on the roadmap, with the re-evaluation scheduled before them.

Labs announce releases, but the capabilities that matter to your product often show up unannounced: a point release that suddenly handles your long documents, a cheaper tier that becomes good enough for a task you priced out, an agent that now finishes the 40-step workflow it used to abandon at step 12. You find out by testing. A roadmap built on fixed dates for fixed capabilities will be wrong in both directions.

Gate items on evals

Write capability-dependent items as triggers: “When a model passes our contract-extraction eval at 95% pass^3 under $0.05 a document, ship automated extraction to the mid-market tier.” The trigger is testable, the team knows what to watch, and leadership sees why the date is uncertain. This is the roadmap form of the capability watch list from the first lesson.

HorizonWhat goes thereCommitmentGate
NowFeatures that meet their eval threshold on today’s modelDatedEval passes today
NextFeatures at 60–80% of threshold where the gap is model capabilityBuilt behind a flag, undated launchEval threshold on a new model, with a cost ceiling
LaterBets that need a capability jump or a new market conditionPrototype and eval onlyExplicit trigger, reviewed each quarter
Kill listItems made obsolete or unviableStoppedThe kill criterion that fired

Rituals that keep it honest

  • New-model run within a week. Every significant release gets your full eval suite and your watch list. Chapter 14 makes this a recurring model upgrade day.
  • Quarterly “what got easier” review. List compensating scaffolding that can now be removed and watch-list items that crossed threshold. Deletions count as roadmap progress.
  • Kill criteria on every bet. Written before work starts: a date, a threshold or a market signal at which you stop. Without them, AI bets run on hope for quarters.
  • Capacity held back. Keep a slice of each quarter unallocated so the team can take advantage of a capability jump without breaking other commitments. Size it from how often your watch list has crossed thresholds before.

Two failure modes

Over-committing: promising a launch date for a feature whose quality depends on a model that doesn’t exist yet. Under-reacting: a new model makes a planned three-month build a two-day prompt change and nobody notices for a quarter because nothing was set up to test it.

What changes for you

  • Rewrite capability-dependent roadmap items as eval triggers with a quality threshold and a cost ceiling.
  • Put kill criteria on every Next and Later item, written before work starts.
  • Hold back explicit capacity each quarter for capability jumps, and report how it was used.

lessons.t: Telling a credible AI story to leadership
lessons.html:
Leadership hears two stories about AI every week. One says it will change everything and they are falling behind. The other says it’s overhyped and the pilots aren’t paying back. A credible AI story sits between them, with specific bets, measured results, honest costs and explicit conditions for stopping.

Weak claimCredible version
“We added AI to six features”“Ticket deflection rose from 18% to 27% on the AI path over eight weeks, with CSAT flat. The other five features haven’t moved a metric yet; two are on the kill list.”
“The model is 95% accurate”“On a 300-case eval built from real tickets, 91% of cases pass on three of three runs. The failures cluster in refunds over $500, which now route to a human.”
“AI will cut costs”“Cost per resolved ticket is $0.42 at the median and $3.10 at the 95th percentile. Gross margin on the tier is 64%, rising if the next model keeps current quality at a lower price.”
“We have a data moat”“Edits from 40,000 accepted drafts raised our eval pass rate by 6 points. A competitor starting today would need a year of usage to collect them.”
“We’re watching OpenAI”“If a lab ships this as a first-party feature, we keep the integration with the ticketing system and the approval workflow. Here is what we would stop doing.”

All numbers in the table are illustrative. The pattern is what matters: a metric leadership already cares about, a baseline, a measured change, the cost, and what you’d do if it stalled.

A structure that works

  1. The user problem and the business metric it moves. Start here, never with the model.
  2. What we measured. Offline evals and online metrics (Chapter 5), including the failure cases.
  3. Economics. Cost per user at median and heavy usage, and margin (Chapter 11).
  4. Risk. The launch review outcome and residual risks accepted (Chapter 12).
  5. What better models change. Which bets they unlock and which work they make obsolete.
  6. The bets, with kill criteria. Three to five, each with a trigger and a stop condition.
  7. The ask. People, budget, data access or a decision, stated plainly.

Questions you will get

  • “What if the lab builds this?” Answer from the moats lesson. Name what they would lack.
  • “Why aren’t we using AI more?” Show the watch list and the triggers. It shows you are testing continuously and committing only where it pays.
  • “What percentage of our code is AI-written?” Redirect to outcomes: cycle time, defect rates, review load (Chapter 8). Activity metrics invite the wrong targets.

Vanity metrics to avoid

Token volume, number of AI features, share of code written by agents and pilot counts all measure activity. Leaders who are given activity metrics will set activity targets, and teams will hit them without moving the business.

What changes for you

  • Lead every AI update with a business metric, its baseline and the measured change, then cost, then risk.
  • Present bets with kill criteria, and report the ones you killed. It builds more credibility than another launch.
  • Prepare a written answer to “what if the lab builds this?” before anyone asks.

lab.title: Stress-test your roadmap against a better model
lab.intro: Assume a model twice as capable at half the price arrives next quarter. Sort your roadmap into what it kills, what it leaves alone and what it unlocks, then check the unlocked items against today’s best model so the bets are grounded.
steps: List the roadmap. Take 10–20 items from your current and next quarter, including non-AI work. One line each, with the estimated effort.
Label the scaffolding. For each AI item, mark whether its main work is compensating scaffolding (working around model weakness) or durable (integration, evals, workflow, data, UX for review).

Apply the 2× model. Classify each item as obsolete (the model does it unaided), cheaper (same work, lower cost or effort), unchanged, or unlocked (newly viable). Write one sentence of reasoning per item.

Probe the top three unlocked items. Run today’s best available model on 10 realistic tasks for each, using your Chapter 5 eval style. Record pass rate over three runs and cost per task. This tells you how far away each item is.
Name the moat per item. For every item you keep, write which source from the moats lesson it builds: workflow, distribution, data, evals or trust. Items with none are candidates to buy, wrap or drop.
Rewrite as triggers and kill criteria. Move items between Now, Next, Later and the kill list. Give each Next and Later item an eval trigger with a cost ceiling, and every bet a kill criterion.
Review with one peer. Spend 20 minutes with an engineer or PM from another team who challenges the obsolete and unlocked calls. Change at least one classification or record why you didn’t.
lab.template: ItemEffortCompensating or durableUnder a 2× modelProbe result (pass^3, cost)Moat builtNew horizonTriggerKill criterion
lab.done: Every roadmap item has a classification and a reason. At least one item has moved to the kill list or been cut down because a better model makes it unnecessary. The three unlocked items have measured distance from viability. Every Next and Later item has a testable trigger and a kill criterion, ready for the one-page strategy.

quiz.q: Your team spent a quarter building a seven-step prompt chain that decomposes contract review. A new model handles the task better in a single call. What should you do?
o: Keep the chain, because it represents significant investment
Fine-tune the old model to match the new one
Run both on your eval, and if the single call wins on quality and cost, remove the chain and keep the eval
Add the new model as an eighth step in the chain
quiz.w: The chain was compensating scaffolding. Sunk cost isn’t a reason to keep it. The eval is the durable asset and tells you when to delete.

quiz.q: A competitor uses the same model and has a larger engineering team. Which of your assets is hardest for them to copy within a year?
o: Your system prompt
Your choice of model provider
Your chat UI
Deep integration with customers’ systems of record plus outcome data from accepted and edited drafts
quiz.w: Prompts, UI and model choice can be copied quickly. Workflow integration and outcome data tied to real decisions take time and customers to build.

quiz.q: A lead says, “We have ten years of support tickets, so we have a data moat.” What is the best response?
o: Ask which eval improved, by how much, when that data was used, and whether a rival could get similar data
Agree, because more data always means better models
Disagree, because data never matters with foundation models
Suggest pretraining a model on the tickets
quiz.w: Data is a moat only when it measurably improves quality and is hard to replicate. Volume alone usually isn’t enough.

quiz.q: Your roadmap includes “automated invoice matching, Q3”. Today’s best model passes 72% of your eval for it, and the failures are reasoning failures on multi-line invoices. How should the item be written?
o: Keep Q3 and add engineers
Move it to Next, build behind a flag, and gate launch on a trigger such as 95% pass^3 under a set cost per invoice
Delete it, since models can’t do it
Fine-tune a model and keep Q3
quiz.w: The gap is model capability, so the honest commitment is an eval trigger. Building behind a flag lets you ship within days of a model that crosses the threshold.

quiz.q: You depend on one provider’s model and two of its proprietary API features. What is the cheapest, most effective hedge against platform risk?
o: Self-host an open-weight model immediately
Avoid all provider-specific features
Sign a multi-year contract
Keep a portable eval suite and a thin model interface, and run a second provider in shadow on sample traffic
quiz.w: A portable eval and a thin interface make switching an engineering task. Shadow traffic keeps your fallback’s quality and cost known. The other options are costly or give up real gains.

quiz.q: The CEO asks for a quarterly AI update. Which headline will build the most credibility?
o: “Agents now write 60% of our code”
“We launched eight AI features this quarter”
“AI resolution raised first-contact resolution from 41% to 52% at $0.30 per ticket; we killed two features that didn’t move a metric”
“Our token usage tripled”
quiz.w: It ties AI to a business metric with a baseline, gives the cost, and shows discipline through kill decisions. The others measure activity.

deliverable.title: One-page AI strategy
deliverable.html:
One page, for your leadership and your team. Revisit it each quarter and after any major model release.

  1. The user problem and the metric. Who we serve, the job AI helps them do, and the one or two business metrics we will move, with baselines.
  2. Where we win. Our moats by source (workflow, distribution, data, evals, trust), each with its test question and current evidence.
  3. Assumptions about the frontier. What we expect models to do in six and twelve months, stated as eval thresholds and cost per task, and how we will check.
  4. Bets. Three to five. For each: the expected outcome, its horizon (Now, Next, Later), the eval trigger with a cost ceiling, the kill criterion, and the owner.
  5. What we will not build. Capabilities we will buy or leave to platforms, and why.
  6. Dependencies and platform risk. Providers, the features we rely on, deprecation dates, and the fallback for each.
  7. Economics and risk. Cost per user at median and heavy usage, target margin (Chapter 11), and residual risks accepted (Chapter 12).
  8. Review cadence. The new-model run, the quarterly “what got easier” review, and who updates this page.
  9. The ask. People, budget, data access or decisions needed this quarter.

If a bet has no kill criterion or a moat has no evidence, mark it as an open question. Leadership will trust the page more for saying so.
